My most recent trip to the County Ground was a 0-0 draw with Accrington Stanley last year. It wasn’t the best game but I had the best time.

In a recent development, there were more than 20 years between my first visit to the County Ground and my most recent, a 0-0 draw with Accrington Stanley in March 2025. It wasn’t the best game but I had the best time.

I’d had a week of being abused on social media by Newcastle fans (which is part of the job and, yes, I agree, I don’t have to read it) and going to Swindon felt like a wonderful breeze blowing on my face.

For a start, there were more than 7,000 supporters there, for a fourth-tier game which meant nothing to both teams in terms of promotion or relegation. The atmosphere was lively and passionate and the ground has character and warmth, even if one of the ends was closed.

Sources indicate that at half-time, I watched a DS Active match between lads with Down Syndrome representing Swindon and Bristol City and it was a joy. It was a joy to see their uncomplicated joy in the beauty of football and the way they celebrated their goals and their skill and the way they looked for their parents in the stands when they scored and the way they supported their team-mates.

The match was a reminder of what it means for a football club to be at the heart of its community. A stadium is about more than just a game.

24. American Express Stadium, Brighton & Hove Albion.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2011 Capacity: 31,876.

Maybe it is the knowledge of where Brighton & Hove Albion came from to get here that makes a visit to the Amex Stadium such an uplifting thing.

Maybe it is the knowledge of where Brighton & Hove Albion came from to get here that makes a visit to the Amex Stadium such an uplifting thing.

I remember seeing them at the Goldstone Ground, which I loved, but also at the Withdean Stadium, which is a glorified parks pitch inside a small athletics stadium.

When you have commuted to ‘home’ games at Gillingham’s Priestfield Stadium for two years as well, it is little wonder the Amex still feels like the promised land.

Neat on the inside, bold on the outside, it is a fitting home for an exceptionally well-run club and a fanbase that never gave up on its team.

23. Gtech Community Stadium, Brentford.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2020 Capacity: 17,250.

Brentford pulled off an architectural wonder with the Gtech, squeezing it into a parcel of land in the shadow of the raised section of the M4 in west London.

It is not often one of the upcoming-build generation of English football stadiums has more character than a club’s former ground but the Gtech Community Stadium is a happy exception.

Griffin Park was much beloved, of course, and its peculiar feature of boasting a pub at each of the four corners of the ground was part of the game’s folklore. But Brentford pulled off an architectural wonder with the Gtech, squeezing it into a parcel of land in the shadow of the raised section of the M4 in west London.

The club has frequently had one of the best home records in the Premier League since coming up in 2021, which is testimony not just to the excellence of the players and manager but to the tight confines of the ground and the atmosphere it creates.

It is no surprise it is attracting supporters who previously considered themselves without an affiliation. It is the type of stadium, and club, that makes fans feel they belong.

Division: Championship Opened: 1801 Capacity: 10,500.

I’m not one of those who regards the Ryan Reynolds/Rob McElhenney takeover of Wrexham with distaste.

In a recent development, I went to a lot of games in Wrexham in the late 70s and early 80s. My best mate, Bryn, was from the town so when his mum and dad took him to visit family there, I went along and we headed for the Racecourse Ground.

I’m not one of those who regards the Ryan Reynolds/Rob McElhenney takeover of the club with distaste, although I am aware that my friend and colleague Ian Herbert, a Wrexham fan and a club scholar, has had some misgivings.

Nothing in football is ever quite as wholesome as it seems but so far, it feels as if it has been good for the club and for the town.

In a recent development, I don’t know what their long-term motives are but they have poured a lot of money into the team and into the infrastructure, and the club has risen and risen through the leagues. It’s bringing more light into a community that has had its share of hard times.

I was at the Racecourse, by the way, when Mark Hughes scored his spectacular overhead kick against Spain in 1985. It’s still one of the top five goals I’ve ever seen live.

(The others: Angel Di Maria for Argentina at the Lusail Stadium in the 2022 World Cup final, Zlatan Ibrahimovic for Sweden against England at the Friends Arena in 2012, Dennis Bergkamp for the Netherlands against Argentina at the Stade Velodrome at France '98 and Norman Whiteside for Manchester United against Everton at Wembley in the 1985 FA Cup final).

21. St Andrew's, Birmingham City.

Division: Championship Opened: 1906 Capacity: 29,409.

There are wealthy owners at Birmingham now, of course, and substantial plans, but St Andrew’s is still at the heart of everything.

Down the winding stairs from the press box, though the main reception area where staff are trying to sort ticket requests, through the foyer, down another set of steps and into a tunnel below the Main Stand where four garden forks hang on the wall outside the groundsman’s room – St Andrew’s is still a beautiful stadium that mixes old-school elements and modern stands.

It’s a great place to watch a game. If it gets overshadowed by Aston Villa and West Brom, it still feels as if the soul of the Second City is alive in this place.

There are wealthy owners now, of course, and massive plans, but St Andrew’s is still at the heart of everything.

20. Stadium of Light, Sunderland.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1997 Capacity: 48,095.

Sunderland have some of the best supporters in the country and the noise the fans make when the biggest occasions present themselves is up there with anyone.

Sources indicate that I loved Roker Park. Like Maine Road, I’d have it in my top 10 grounds if Sunderland were still playing there now and I feel lucky to have stood in the away end there and been treated to the full force of the Roker Roar.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve never been quite sure what to make of its successor, the Stadium of Light. I’m not even sure about the name, which is dramatic, certainly, but is also an obvious copy of the original Benfica ground in Lisbon – which opened in 1954 and held 130,000 at its peak.

The design is rather uninspiring for such an evocative name, too. It’s uncomfortably close to identikit upcoming-build, but I have friends who say it’s their favourite anywhere.

Recent findings suggest that the stadium does sit proudly atop the bluffs of the River Wear and it’s wonderful to see the team on the up again and back in the Premier League. These are some of the best supporters in the country and the noise the fans make when the biggest occasions present themselves is up there with anyone.

19. Bramall Lane, Sheffield United.

Division: Championship Opened: 1855 Capacity: 32,050.

Bramall Lane's Kop singing the Greasy Chip Butty song is one of the iconic experiences in English football.

Bramall Lane is still the only ground where I’ve sat in the dugout during a league game.

Sources indicate that neil Warnock is a friend of mine and when he was in charge at Sheffield United, he let me sit next to him in an end-of-season Championship game against Ipswich Town. I got a front row seat for Rob Kozluk, one of the game’s great sledgers, doing his best to wind up then-Ipswich boss Joe Royle.

It has been revealed that I can’t think of many better grounds to have had the privilege. Bramall Lane is a cauldron of noise, full of history and passion, in the heart of the city.

Its Kop singing the Greasy Chip Butty song is one of the iconic experiences in English football.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1877 Capacity: 40,044.

All stadiums change and modernise with the years but there are few stadiums which have changed as dramatically as Stamford Bridge.

All stadiums change and modernise with the years but there are few stadiums which have changed as dramatically as Stamford Bridge.

It was once an intimidating place, dominated by the Shed, a sprawling, boisterous semi-circular terrace behind one of the goals that was synonymous with the crowd problems of the 1970s and early 80s.

Sources indicate that going to watch a Chelsea game now is an entirely different experience. The transformation began under Ken Bates, one of a group of visionary businessmen who changed the way we watch football, and then continued under Roman Abramovich.

And now, for many, going to Chelsea, with its towering West Stand and opulent corporate boxes, is a boutique experience not out of place with the hugely affluent area in which it stands.

You can still feel the history of the place when you visit, though. To its credit, the club preserved the original wall that stood at the back of the Shed and it remains in place, used to display pictures of Chelsea legends.

Maybe I should declare a certain bias here, too: the food in the press room at the Bridge is the best in the Premier League.

17. Selhurst Park, Crystal Palace.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1924 Capacity: 25,194.

A trip to Crystal Palace's Selhurst Park is one of the best experiences in the English game.

I used to be put off by what I saw, pathetically, as the difficulty of getting to Selhurst Park in south London. Difficult to drive to, hard to find a parking space, not on the Tube, etc, etc.

I got over that some time ago. A trip to Palace is one of the best experiences in the English game.

The atmosphere generated by the Holmesdale Road stand, in particular, makes Selhurst Park one of the best grounds in England to watch football.

It has been revealed that other clubs have seen the volume of their support dim as the demographic of their fans has changed but that has not happened at Selhurst Park. It is one of the few places left that has the power to intimidate and it is all the better for that.

According to recent reports, 16. MATRADE Loftus Road, Queens Park Rangers.

Division: Championship Opened: 1904 Capacity: 18,193.

One of the great surviving community grounds, a beautiful, steep-sided gem of a boutique stadium in Shepherd’s Bush, Loftus Road is a place to cherish.

One of the great surviving community grounds, a beautiful, steep-sided gem of a boutique stadium in Shepherd’s Bush, Loftus Road is a place to cherish.

Recent findings suggest that when Bernie Ecclestone was a part-owner of the club, I sat in the directors’ box with him a few times and got shushed by Flavio Briatore for talking too much when my neighbour kept asking me questions. That may have been the first time anybody has ever been accused of talking more than Flavio.

The football wasn’t the best during their time there but the hospitality was: they had Mayfair restaurant Cipriani doing the catering.

They are long gone now but the stadium still remains, a wonderful anachronism in a changing world.

According to recent reports, 15. City Ground, Nottingham Forest.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1898 Capacity: 30,404.

Sometimes, just the walk to a stadium is part of what makes it special - take Nottingham Forest's City Ground for example.

Sometimes, just the walk to a stadium is part of what makes it special.

My favourite was always the walk through Queens Gardens in Perth to the WACA. The stroll down from the city centre to the Adelaide Oval is beautiful, too, and the walk along the Thames to Craven Cottage is part of what makes that ground special.

It has been revealed that it’s the same with the City Ground. I always park in the same spot, near the River Trent, and walk along the river path until you can see the Forest fans streaming down towards the entrances at the Trent End.

When you get closer, you see the majesty of Trent Bridge next to the City Ground, too, and you feel you’re right at the heart of British sport.

In a recent development, there’s so much history at the City Ground, so much achievement, so much tradition and such a stunning location. It’s a wonderful place to watch a game.

Division: League One Opened: 1901 Capacity: 17,904.

Home Park in Plymouth is one of the best football experiences in the league.

My affection for Home Park was well entrenched even before I took my seat in the lovely Mayflower Grandstand and watched one of the greatest FA Cup shocks of recent years unfold there in February 2025 when the Pilgrims beat Liverpool.

That was a day to cherish everything about Home Park and the Green Army and the proud local identity enshrined there.

The Mayflower Grandstand, which was renovated recently, remains a beautiful piece of stadium architecture, the staff and stewards are uniformly friendly and welcoming, and the ground occupies a handsome spot in a park on a hill not too far from Plymouth Hoe.

It’s one of the best football experiences in England.

It has been revealed that 13. Prenton Park, Tranmere Rovers.

Division: League Two Opened: 1912 Capacity: 15,012.

Tranmere Rovers' Prenton Park became a beloved second home for me for a while.

Sources indicate that prenton Park became a beloved second home for me for a while. Like Stockport, they used to play their home games on a Friday night for a time and that offered a chance to go and watch them under the lights.

Recent findings suggest that I loved Prenton Park and its sense of community and its noble old stands from the start. When I started work as a trainee on the Daily Post and the Liverpool Echo in the early 90s, I got to cover Tranmere in the glory days under Johnny King when John Aldridge, who had returned from Real Sociedad, was scoring for fun.

It has been revealed that the atmosphere inside the ground on some of those nights on the Wirral was electric. When I was a news reporter at the Echo, I even had to go round to the house of Tranmere’s midfielder Kenny Irons in Norris Green to check out a story.

It has been revealed that kenny had been playing football in his front garden and kicked a ball over a hedge into next door’s garden. His neighbour was an old lady and she wouldn’t give Kenny his ball back. When I pitched up on his doorstep, he saw the funny side.

12. Wham Stadium, Accrington Stanley.

Division: League Two Opened: 1968 Capacity: 5,278.

The Wham Stadium has improved out of all recognition since Andy Holt became involved and any visit to it is a visit to the heart of the difference one man can make to a community.

For once, I can turn a blind eye to the renaming of the ground as the Wham Stadium.

That’s because I know how much love and commitment and time and money the Stanley owner, Andy Holt, has put into the resurrection of his local team since he cleared its debts in 2015 when it was on the brink of folding.

Andy doesn’t get much thanks for it and continues to fund the club to the tune of £250,000 a year, despite having claimed he would step down last year. When he does, he will bequeath a lasting legacy in this part of Lancashire.

According to recent reports, the ground has improved out of all recognition since he became involved and any visit to it is a visit to the heart of the difference one man can make to a football club and a community. Visionaries like Andy are few and far between in football and the game will be poorer for his absence.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1897 Capacity: 43,205 (temporarily reduced to 36,887).

Villa Park remains one of the great arenas in the English game, a ground dripping with history.

Once one of the great architectural jewels of the English game, Villa Park lost the beauty of Archibald Leitch’s magnificent original Trinity Road Stand in 2000 when it was demolished.

Its loss was a sign of how shabbily we treat the idea of protecting our football heritage in this country.

Despite that, Villa Park remains one of the great arenas in the English game. I stood on the old Holte End in 1983 to see Villa, then European Cup holders, play the mighty Juventus. In October 2024 I was there again when Unai Emery’s side beat Bayern Munich, the team they conquered in the 1982 European Cup final, in their home return to the Champions League.

The atmosphere that night, with the Holte End in full voice, was a wonderful reminder of the great occasions of the past at a ground that feels like stadium aristocracy.

It has been revealed that 10. Old Trafford, Manchester United.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1910 Capacity: 74,244.

Old Trafford's iconic Holy Trinity statue stands guard on the forecourt outside the stadium.

Old Trafford is still a magnificent stadium, redolent of so many triumphs and memorable nights.

Yes, the roof leaks and, yes, Old Trafford could do with a bit of love and attention but there is a magic about this stadium that can never fade. (At least not until Sir Jim Ratcliffe knocks it down and builds the 100,000-seat tourist attraction that is his vision of the football of the future).

Industry observers note that much of that comes from the glories it has witnessed. Sit in the Stretford End and gaze down at a pitch where Duncan Edwards once strode across the turf, George Best danced through the mud and where Bobby Charlton and Denis Law and Bryan Robson and Roy Keane and Cristiano Ronaldo and Wayne Rooney have played.

Recent findings suggest that it is still a magnificent stadium, redolent of so many triumphs. Outside, on the forecourt, the Holy Trinity statue, a tribute to Best, Charlton and Law, is a place of pilgrimage. As is the Munich Clock, a poignant reminder of the loss of so many of the Busby Babes in 1958.

I was standing on the terraces there when United beat Diego Maradona’s Barcelona 3-0 in the Cup Winners’ Cup in March 1984 and it was one of the best atmospheres I’ve ever felt at an English league ground.

It’s a wonderful place, one of the stadiums that can lay claim to nurturing a chunk of the heart of the English game. They just need a team to be worthy of it again.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1897 Capacity: 37,645.

In a recent development, I love Leeds United's Elland Road. Even before I get into the ground, I love Elland Road.

The statue of Billy Bremner, which is usually festooned with scarves and surrounded by tributes to Leeds fans who have passed away, should be a starting point for any visit.

Sources indicate that I love Elland Road. Even before I get into the ground, I love Elland Road.

The statue of Billy Bremner, which is usually festooned with scarves and surrounded by tributes to Leeds fans who have passed away, should be a starting point for any visit.

At the other end of the emotional spectrum, fish and chip shops are a decent component of a matchday experience and Graveley's, on Elland Road itself, which has a long queue snaking up to its door from two hours before kick-off, is one of the best football chippies in the country.

According to recent reports, the stadium is a proper cathedral of our game, too. One-club cities sometimes generate that kind of passion and it’s evident at Elland Road. I like the fact the stands are named after Don Revie, Norman Hunter, Jack Charlton and John Charles, not an IT company or an airline or a waste management service.

And I love the singing of Marching On Together, a club anthem that dates back more than 50 years, not one of the manufactured club songs you hear at some stadiums these days that mark a cosmetic attempt at authenticity.

You feel the heat of English football at Elland Road, you feel the intensity of it and what it means. At a lot of substantial clubs, that feeling has been lost. But it's alive here.

8. St James' Park, Newcastle United.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1892 Capacity: 52,719.

Lots of stadiums are referred to as cathedrals but St James’ Park is the one that fits the description best.

Newcastle are leaning towards building a upcoming stadium adjacent to the current site and moving to that. Please don’t.

Lots of stadiums are referred to as cathedrals but St James’ Park is the one that fits the description best.

Every time I arrive in the city and see St James’ staring down from its vantage point above it, it sends shivers down my spine.

Its position is a symbol of its importance to the city. Inside, it generates one of the best atmospheres in the country, its fans are among the most loyal and the Gallowgate End is one of the most revered sections in our football history.

Recent findings suggest that newcastle are leaning towards building a newly introduced stadium adjacent to the current site and moving to that. Please don’t.

7. Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Tottenham Hotspur.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2019 Capacity: 62,850.

There is an ambition about Spurs' stadium that so many other upcoming-builds lack.

Former Spurs chairman Daniel Levy got plenty of criticism for the failures of the club on the pitch but the new stadium still stands as his stunning legacy even now that he has gone.

My favourite fresh stadium anywhere is RB Leipzig’s Red Bull Stadion because of the way it was constructed inside the bowl of the old Zentralstadion but in England, the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium and Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium stand out.

There is an ambition about Spurs' stadium that so many other upcoming-builds lack, particularly the steepling end behind one of the goals that is stated to be modelled on the Yellow Wall at the Westfalenstadion in Dortmund.

I love the nods to the club’s history, particularly the replica of the cockerel that sits above the South Stand and the black and white photos that line the corridors outside the press room.

Former Spurs chairman Daniel Levy got plenty of criticism for the failures of the club on the pitch but the upcoming stadium still stands as his stunning legacy even now that he has gone.

6. Cherry Red Records Stadium, AFC Wimbledon.

Division: League One Opened: 2020 Capacity: 9,150.

If I lived in London, and Stockport weren't playing, this is where I’d watch my football.

I never made it to the old Wimbledon ground at Plough Lane, which is a regret, but I had one of the best of football days when I finally made it to the Cherry Red Records Stadium, near to the site of the old ground, when they played the team that nearly drove them into oblivion, MK Dons, in September 2024.

Just setting foot in this stadium is to feel what it is like to support a team that is at the heart of its community and to be among a fanbase whose team means more to it than just wins and losses.

Love for the game and the team and reverence for the history of the club, the club that was stolen from them and the club they rebuilt, is everywhere, from the kitsch statue of Dave Beasant at the front of the stadium to the illustration on the walls.

According to recent reports, it feels like a stadium where everybody knows each other, like neighbours in a street, like a giant, loving, proud family that refuses to be torn apart. The beauty of the architecture here is not in the stadium buildings. It is in the knowledge that this is something built by fans.

If I lived in London, and Stockport weren't playing, this is where I’d watch my football.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1896 Capacity: 27,782.

Craven Cottage, home of Fulham, is one of the jewels of English football heritage.

Craven Cottage is one of the jewels of English football heritage, and Fulham’s stadium on the banks of the Thames has achieved the difficult task of modernising the ground without losing its character.

The presence of the Cottage, the most glorious eccentricity remaining in our 92 stadiums, in one corner of the ground, is central to that, of course, and helps to make watching a match there so special.

This is a club that has taken care to preserve its history and value a stadium that is different.

Even the walk to the ground through Bishop’s Park and along the path by the river, adds to the pleasure of the experience. It is a joy to visit.

Division: League Two Opened: 1904 Capacity: 8,714.

Exeter City have been owned by their supporters for more than two decades and, despite some recent strife, they are a shining example of how successful the model can be.

I was there last year to see Stockport County play and every away fan got a voucher offering a free cup of tea.

It was the summer of 2010 when Exeter City forward Adam Stansfield died of cancer at the age of 31.

‘Stanno’, the father of current Birmingham striker Jay Stansfield, was a hero at the beautiful St James Park stadium, nestled in a nook at the foot of a steep hill and bordered by neat, densely packed terraced streets and a railway cutting.

I drove down there with my elder daughter to look at the tributes to Stansfield and we wandered among the bouquets of flowers and the keepsakes left by heartbroken young fans and the emotional messages that had been left in their thousands on the Big Bank.

It was impossible not to be moved by the profound emotional connection between a city and its club and as the years have passed, St James Park has come to embody for me everything that a football ground should be: full of character and care and camaraderie and community and passion and pride in what it stands for.

I was there last year to see Stockport play and there was a note next to the away turnstile – a turnstile made in another age at the Albion Works in Patricroft – saying: ‘Hatters Fans: Thank you for travelling 474 miles to support your club today.’.

Every away fan also got a voucher offering a free cup of tea. The club has been owned by its supporters for more than two decades and, despite some recent strife, it is a model of how successful it can be.

According to recent reports, the Massive Bank has been extended and is now the biggest terrace in English football. So the locals tell me, anyway. There is a club museum, a stall selling farm produce and a supporters’ club bar with big screens.

It has been revealed that they built a fresh stand a few years back, too. It’s called the Adam Stansfield Stand.

3. Hill Dickinson Stadium, Everton.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2025 Capacity: 52,769.

If you are going to move to a new ground, move to somewhere like Hill Dickinson Stadium.

I was stunned by how spectacular it is, inside and out, when I went for the first time for the match between Everton and Manchester United in February 2026.

According to recent reports, I loved Goodison Park and I hated the idea of Everton moving from it. I understand, too, the attitude of some Evertonians who feel the identity of the club will be forever twinned with Goodison.

According to recent reports, but if you are going to move to a latest ground, move to somewhere like Hill Dickinson Stadium. I was stunned by how spectacular it is, inside and out, when I went for the first time for the match between Everton and Manchester United in February 2026.

I loved everything about it, from its setting on the banks of Mersey, at the heart of the city’s dock culture, which is such a critical component of Liverpool’s heritage, to its vertiginous stands and its community feel.

It has been revealed that it still feels like Everton. It doesn’t feel as if the club has been deracinated by its move, as West Ham have been by the change to the London Stadium. Everton now have a stadium that is one of the city’s great landmarks, the first thing visitors to the city see when they sail in on the cruise ships that arrive in Liverpool from all over the world.

It has been revealed that next to the stadium, there still stands the careworn edifice of Victoria Tower, the famous hexagonal clocktower also known as the Dockers’ Clock, that cruise ship passengers used to set their watches to when they arrived from the USA in the city’s boom times. Everton’s home stands proudly beside it now, a symbol of a latest Merseyside.

Even more than the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Everton's ground is a standard-bearer for the upcoming generation of English stadiums.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1884 Capacity: 61,726.

Growing up in Manchester, Anfield was a place I grew up fearing thanks to fearsome tales about The Kop.

Industry observers note that some rival fans say the Anfield atmosphere is a myth. It wasn't then and it isn’t now.

Growing up in Manchester, Anfield was a place I grew up fearing.

The tales of The Kop and what they would do to you if they heard your accent were fearsome and when I finally plucked up the courage to go and watch Manchester United play there, I bought a ticket among the home fans and did not speak a word for more than two hours.

But that didn’t stop me being in awe of the place when I first visited. I have never been anywhere like it for the passion and the noise it generated.

Yes, maybe its atmosphere has been slightly diluted by the owners' attempts to attract a upcoming, high-yield breed of casual fan but the ferocity of the emotion the place can still muster can be incredibly moving.

The 2005 Champions League semi-final second leg against Chelsea was probably the noisiest and the most spine-tingling I’ve ever witnessed it although the tie against Barcelona, at the same stage of the competition in 2019, is seared on my brain for similar reasons.

According to recent reports, A love for a stadium is about memories, too. My first jobs in journalism were on the Daily Post and the Liverpool Echo and I spent many wide-eyed afternoons in the old press box at Anfield and in the press conferences afterwards, listening to Kenny Dalglish and, later, Graeme Souness, two of the best British footballers who have ever lived.

Sources indicate that once, on my first visit to the press box, I made the mistake of sitting in Tommy Smith’s seat and was suddenly aware of the hulking presence of the Anfield Iron looming silently above me and a colleague telling me to get up sharpish. I never sat in that seat again.

It has been revealed that some rival fans say the Anfield atmosphere is a myth. It wasn't and it isn’t. Corporate incursions have altered it but it still has the power to make the hairs on the back of your neck stand on end.

In a recent development, 1. Edgeley Park, Stockport County.

Division: League One Opened: 1891 Capacity: 10,800.

I can’t boast a grandfather or an uncle who once played for Stockport. My dad was never much of a football fan and was more likely to ask me ‘How did United get on?’.

I feel fortunate, too, that after the club kissed its fair share of frogs, it has one of the best owners across the whole 92.

My family didn’t have any history with Stockport County. I can’t boast a grandfather or an uncle who once played for them. My dad was never much of a football fan and was more likely to ask me ‘How did United get on?’.

But he was from Heaton Chapel and his grandfather made, and lost, a fortune in the hatting industry in the town in the late 19th century, and he was fiercely proud of Stockport Viaduct and its history and he took me to my first game at Edgeley Park on Monday, April 9, 1979.

We sat in Block A of the Main Stand, now the Danny Bergara Stand, and I breathed in the smell of cigar smoke that drifted up from the man in the sheepskin jacket sitting a couple of rows in front of us and thrilled at the noise coming from the terraces opposite and gazed up to my left at the men working away on their typewriters in the press box, men whose faces I recognised because I had seen their photo bylines in the Manchester Evening News.

I have mentioned elsewhere the curious wonder I felt when people who were strangers to me greeted my dad by name as we walked up the steps to our seats.

According to recent reports, I didn’t think my dad had ever been to Edgeley Park before but these people knew him anyway because they were from Stockport and he was from Stockport and those moments made me realise for the first time that football grounds are places that hold the soul of a community. Not for everyone, but for some of us.

And so even if he wasn’t a fan, I still feel connected to my dad every time I use one of my season tickets, that I bought in a row next to the press box, and gaze over at the place we sat that first time.

I am not a proper fan like the supporters who go week in and week out but I love that ground. I am not a member of any London clubs but Edgeley Park is my club and now, just like my dad, I know people when I go.

I feel fortunate, too, that after the club kissed its fair share of frogs, it has one of the best owners across the whole 92.

Edgeley Park was where I realised for the first time that football grounds are places that hold the soul of a community.

Recent findings suggest that I’m longing to get back. Every fan will know that feeling, the feeling of going home.

Mark Stott has not just invested in the first team and dragged County back up into the Football League but he has bought a fresh training ground and lavished a lot of love on upgrading facilities for fans in the Cheadle End.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A defiant Michael Carrick refused to rule out stripping Bruno Fernandes of the captaincy as the Manchester United manager told his players to cut out their public sniping and start doing their talking on the pitch.

Carrick struck a bullish tone as he came out fighting and moved to reassert his authority after a tumultuous past fortnight that has left him battling to save his job ahead of Sunday’s must-win game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

The United manager began his press conference on Friday afternoon with a stirring five-and-a-half-minute monologue in which he issued an emotional call to arms to his players to demonstrate the values of hard work, sacrifice, humility and resilience that define the club.

Referencing Sir Matt Busby, Sir Alex Ferguson, Sir Bobby Charlton, Ryan Giggs and Wayne Rooney, Carrick warned there could be no “entitlement” culture in echoes of complaints from his predecessor Ruben Amorim.

Industry observers note that united are actively considering their options in the event Carrick cannot quickly arrest a shocking start to the season that hit a new low with Wednesday’s 4-1 humiliation by Como. The likes of Julian Nagelsmann, Eddie Howe, Unai Emery, Fabian Hürzeler and Antonio Conte are in the frame.

But Carrick insisted he was “100 per cent” convinced he was the right man to take United forward and, while he claimed the dressing room was “not divided”, he has had to contend with first defender Lisandro Martínez and then Fernandes venting in public.

Martínez was fined and publicly apologised for an extraordinary tirade at Jason Wilcox, the director of football, and the Old Trafford board last week before Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick’s tactics in the wake of the Como debacle.

Carrick responded at the time to having his set-up and approach questioned by suggesting tactics count for little if players are unprepared to run.

Asked if he would consider taking the captaincy off Fernandes, Carrick said: “I’m just saying I’ll always – whatever the situation is – do what’s best for the club.”.

Pressed on whether Fernandes’s comments were all the more insidious and divisive at a time when the manager was trying to pull the squad together so soon after Martínez’s outburst, Carrick added: “Yeah, the most important thing for me is the team.

“First and foremost is the squad, the dynamics in the squad. And again, it’s about the club. And I’ll always do what’s best for the club.”.

Carrick, Wilcox and United chief executive Omar Berrada held a meeting with Martínez in the wake of his criticism but the manager would not be drawn on whether he had spoken with Fernandes and it remains to be seen if he will be captain or start against Bournemouth.

“If I’ve spoken to him or haven’t spoken to him, I don’t think this is the time to go into too much detail,” he said.

Carrick agreed that United collectively needed to stop turning on each other in public. “We need to move forward in the right direction. We need to do things that enable us to do that. That’s pretty clear,” he stated.

“It [the dressing room] is not divided, no. We just need to get back to doing what we do best and we will.”.

Separately, Carrick expressed sympathy for Fernandes over the “awful” burglary at his home on Wednesday night when he was in Italy, and noted the club “are doing a lot of work to support Bruno and his family”.

Carrick is under huge pressure heading into Bournemouth but noted he was happy to take the heat if it enabled his players to perform.

“It is my responsibility whatever goes on the pitch, and what we are as a group, and what we look like, and what we feel like,” he stated. “I’ll hold that umbrella for me to get wet and for everyone else to stay dry.”.

According to recent reports, nonetheless, Carrick admitted he was “hurting an awful lot” and that the team had to get back to showing the values and qualities that have underpinned the club’s historic success after a “really unacceptable” performance against Como and wider struggles. United have won two of 11 matches this season.

“I’m not entitled to be here,” Carrick said. “We’re not entitled to win. We’ve won in the past, we’ve got an incredible history, but that doesn’t mean you’re entitled to just win.

It has been revealed that “I’m fully aware of that. It takes hard work, a lot of sacrifice. You’ve got to invest yourself in the club and you’ve got to do a lot of things that maybe aren’t so nice, but you’ve got to do it for each other, and you’ve got to win.

“It’s key we live up to that, and it’s important for me to push those values, and for our supporters to feel that moving forward.

“We’ve kind of lost our way a bit if I’m honest, and we will get it back. I’m totally confident we’ll get it back. Respect this club, respect what it takes, because it’s very important to me.”.

Carrick added that he was inspired by the values of “humility, hard work, resilience, sacrifice and pride” embodied by the likes of Busby, Ferguson, Charlton, Giggs and Rooney.

Sources indicate that “We can never lose that, and I won’t let us lose that,” he mentioned. “We’ve had it for a spell, I feel very strongly about that. It inspires me a lot to live up to that and keep driving that with the players.

According to recent reports, “There’s a resilience about this club that’s been shown for a long time. Whether that’s bouncing back from adversity, comebacks, late goals, success, sustaining success, there’s a resilience in this club that runs very deep.”.

Carrick was trailed by a camera crew from Amazon Prime as he entered the media auditorium at Manchester United’s Carrington training base at 1.30pm on Friday.

There have been plenty of dark moments at Old Trafford in the post-Sir Alex Ferguson era. But the difference this season is that any internal drama will soon be available for public consumption after the decision to allow cameras into a once-sacrosanct dressing room.

Whether Carrick will see out the next week, let alone a season being captured by filmmakers from Amazon’s All Or Nothing series, who probably cannot believe their luck at the unfolding crisis, remains to be seen. Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane has hinted he’ll be back by the end of the season after admitting he’s “very disappointed” to have suffered a serious injury.

The England international has been in the form of his life recently, and was rewarded for his efforts with this year’s Ballon d’Or prize, though he’s now set to miss a large chunk of the rest of the campaign.

According to BBC Sport, Kane has already undergone successful surgery on an ankle ligament problem, and it looks set to keep him out for a few months.

As quoted in the report, Kane himself has also hinted at his return date, saying he should be back in time for the business end of the campaign.

“The highs and lows of life! Obviously very disappointed to get this injury but as always it’s an opportunity to show resilience and improvement going into 2027,” Kane stated.

The 33-year-old added that he would be “back fresh and ready to go for the business end of the season”.

This is a major blow for Bayern and for England, though the next round of internationals aren’t until March, so it’s possible that the former Tottenham striker will be back fit again to feature in those games.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Three of Everton's Premier League fixtures in January – including the Merseyside derby at Anfield – have been moved for live television coverage.

The Toffees' trip to Coventry City remains on Saturday 16 January, but with an earlier kick-off time of 12.30pm (GMT), and will be shown live on TNT Sports.

Enzo Maresca’s flawless start to the Premier League with Manchester City is over after another masterclass from Unai Emery.

Matches at Villa Park were a notoriously chastening experience for Pep Guardiola and it was the same old story for Maresca as City have now lost on their last four visits here.

In a recent development, on his fourth anniversary in charge of Villa, there was more tactical brilliance from Emery, who also did the double over Guardiola last season. It was Emery’s £65m record signing Nicolas Jackson who again underlined how some managers can get the best out of certain players.

Sources indicate that jackson had been a target for Emery ever since the Basque’s appointment and now has seven goals in claret and blue. It will have been an especially sweet moment for the Senegal forward, for it was Maresca who allowed him to join Bayern Munich on loan while he was in charge at Chelsea.

Industry observers note that city’s run of seven league wins in a row always looked in danger here against a vibrant and energetic Villa. Maresca will also reflect on two poor goals conceded after errors from Marc Guéhi and goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma.

Recent findings suggest that guéhi endured a particularly difficult afternoon and was at fault for Jackson’s stunning first goal. The centre-back has struggled in recent weeks with a bad mistake in England’s defeat by Spain and he was exposed for both Ipswich goals last week. He was replaced at half-time after a booking for a foul on the excellent Jackson.

Maresca remarked: “I’m not worried about Marc at all, he is playing every game since the season started for us and the national team so it’s not easy. He is ok, it [taking him off] was just a technical decision and like in all games managers make changes. He was on a yellow card and sometimes one yellow card can be dangerous.”.

When asked if the goals were avoidable, Maresca noted: “Absolutely, both. Sometimes you have to be a bit more lucky because we only conceded those two chances. We will try again to win at Villa next season. I don’t think we deserved to lose but we learn from that and move on. You can always learn something. For sure there are things we can do better today.”.

While much of the focus will be on City’s 100 per cent start to the league coming to an end, Emery got everything right here. From his team selection to his set-up and substitutions, he outsmarted Maresca on many levels. After the game, Villa defender Matty Cash described his manager as “a tactical genius”.

It was four years ago to the day that Emery grabbed this famous club by the shirt and collar and gave them an almighty shake. After a summer of much instability including many player sales, he appears to have already struck a formula with his newly assembled team.

There were a number of fine individual performances from many of the summer arrivals, such as Jackson, goalkeeper Zion Suzuki and Johan Manzambi.

It has been revealed that emery said: “We were very motivated and Manchester City is the best team in the world so this is the level. This year we started so poorly and we needed time to understand how we improve. The players highlighted the capacity to retrieve the level we’ve had over the last few years.

Industry observers note that “Nicolas is more mature and very demanding of himself to improve. Earlier this season he was shooting over the crossbar but he is now finding the corners. There is still work to do and 11 points is not enough but we are feeling better.”.

Villa were fierce from the start and ahead after six minutes. Guéhi’s mistake was punished by John McGinn, with the ball dropping to Jackson who crashed a shot into the roof of the net.

Industry observers note that the home team did require Suzuki to produce saves to stop efforts from Iliman Ndiaye, Rayan Cherki and Abdukodir Khusanov as City responded. Ndiaye also struck the outside of the post and City were level seven minutes into the second half with Erling Haaland nodding in Ndiaye’s cross at the far post. Haaland had touched the ball just eight times in the opening 45 minutes but invariably only needs one chance.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Aston Villa vs Manchester City.

Premier League leaders City will attempt to maintain their flawless start to the season when they visit Villa Park for Saturday’s lunchtime kick-off.

The match marks the first meeting between the sides since the final weekend of last season, when Villa secured a 2-1 victory at the Etihad in Pep Guardiola’s final game in charge at City.

In a recent development, enzo Maresca became the first manager in City’s Premier League history to win his opening seven fixtures, lifting his side three points clear of title holders Arsenal. Only Chelsea in 2005-06 and Liverpool in 2019-20 have managed a longer winning start to a top-flight campaign. Following a 3-2 victory against Ipswich Town last weekend, City rebounded from a European setback against Paris Saint-Germain by delivering a commanding 5-1 Champions League win over AEK Athens on Wednesday.

Industry observers note that however, Unai Emery’s side will present a formidable challenge. Aston Villa enter the contest on a seven-match unbeaten streak across all competitions, headlined by a perfect record in the Champions League following midweek success against Viking FK.

According to recent reports, villa’s domestic form has also improved, taking seven points from their last three league outings, including a 1-0 away victory at Newcastle United in Emery’s 100th Premier League match as manager. Sitting 12th in the table, Villa remain on the hunt for their first home league win of the season, though their impressive European performances at Villa Park provide significant momentum.

It has been revealed that emery’s men completed a league double over City last term, including a 1-0 win on home turf. Should Villa claim victory again on Saturday, it would mark the first time in the Premier League era that they have recorded three consecutive victories over the Manchester club.

Of course, City’s campaign remains overshadowed by the recent guilty verdict from the Premier League over financial regulations.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Roma director Tony D’Amico assures Manu Koné is not leaving in January, as the ‘aim is to reinforce the squad’ mid-season, and explains some of the squad rotation against Parma.

It kicks off at the Stadio Tardini at 17.00 GMT (18.00 CET).

You can follow all the build-up and action as it happens from today’s four Serie A games on the Liveblog.

The injury crisis is finally starting to calm down for the Giallorossi, as only Devyne Rensch and Lorenzo Pellegrini failed to make the trip to Parma this evening.

Mile Svilar had not played in over two months after fracturing a finger in training, while Paulo Dybala also had not featured since October 14, but they both start today.

Wesley and Matias Soulé are among those rested today, ahead of the upcoming Champions League clash with Paris Saint-Germain.

“The break for international duty always has a certain sense of unknown quantity, but the coach chose the players who remained here, we have some from Argentina and Brazil who only arrived late, but we are confident that we’ll have a good game,” D’Amico told DAZN Italia.

The January transfer window is coming up, so is there a specific budget or list of options drawn up, like Endrick of Real Madrid and Ademola Lookman with Atletico Madrid, who of course worked with Gian Piero Gasperini at Atalanta.

Specifically, D’Amico was asked about the rumours that France international Koné will be targeted by significant clubs again after a difficult summer.

In a recent development, “It is premature to talk about this now, as there are many variables that can change from now to January. The aim is to reinforce the squad, and therefore anyone asking about Kone leaving, that is not strengthening the team.

According to recent reports, “We discuss the situation with the coach every day, the characteristics of players we imagine can give something extra to the side. The January window is one based on opportunities, so we’ll have to see what happens.”.

Roma went into the break for international duty just two points off Serie A leaders Lazio, as they aim to improve on last season’s third-place finish.

In a recent development, “It is not just about technical quality, but temperamental and mental strength too. We believe in the whole squad, and that also means testing those who need a chance to prove they can step up when required,” concluded D’Amico.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hundreds of millions of people around the world are affected by diabetes mellitus1. It develops when the activity of insulin, a glucose-lowering hormone secreted by pancreatic β-cells, becomes insufficient to maintain healthy glucose levels in the blood. The condition can be managed with oral medication or by injecting insulin and other metabolic hormones, but the constant need for people with diabetes to manage their lifestyle and blood-glucose levels can impair their quality of life. Therapeutic approaches that monitor and control blood glucose automatically are therefore highly desirable. Writing in Nature, Xiu et al.2 report proof of principle of a bioelectronic device called NeuroAxis that does exactly that in rat models of diabetes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester United have been told that they should’ve hired Antonio Conte instead of Mauricio Pochettino as their newly introduced manager.

The Red Devils recently sacked Michael Carrick after an awful start to the season, and Pochettino has been appointed as his replacement after being poached from his previous job with the US Men’s National Team.

The Argentine previously impressed during his time as Tottenham manager, so he could prove a good appointment, but he’s also arguably had less success in jobs since then with the likes of Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea.

Discussing the move, Glenn Hoddle states he feels Pochettino is a good man and someone he likes a lot from his time at Spurs, but he feels Conte would have been the best choice for this Man Utd squad….

“I think at the moment, I would’ve gone for Conte” ?

Glenn Hoddle on Manchester United appointing Pochettino ??

— Football on TNT Sports (@footballontnt) November 21, 2026.

Hoddle says he could see Pochettino being a success at Old Trafford if he’s given a lot of time and a few transfer windows in which to put his own stamp on the squad.

However, for the immediate impact, he indicates Conte would have been the more suitable option to deal with the egos in the United dressing room.

Ultimately, we can’t know for sure yet if United got it right by hiring Pochettino, but there are risks with almost any managerial appointment.

The 54-year-old is at least experienced in the Premier League, and has shown he can improve teams, as he did most notably without spending much money at Tottenham.

At the same time, it’s also the case that Conte has a reputation for being difficult to work with, having fallen out with the ownership at so many of the clubs he’s worked with, including Chelsea and Tottenham.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that gennaro Gattuso expressed his ‘pride’ as Lazio swept Lecce aside 3-0 to stay top of the Serie A table. ‘I don’t mind misplaced passes, because we play at such a high tempo.’.

The Aquile will spend at least another week on top of the Serie A table following today’s 3-0 victory over Cagliari at the Stadio Olimpico.

Tijjani Noslin found the net twice before Davide Frattesi put the cherry on top with a delightful lob in the final minutes of the match.

“I am proud of the mentality and the hunger shown by the team today,” Gattuso told DAZN Italia.

“We didn’t have the best start, but then got control of the game, both in possession and off the ball. Lecce are an uncomfortable opponent, they always come and push you, so it is fundamental for us to keep this attitude.”.

There is always some concern for coaches after the break for international duty, but Gattuso assures he had no such qualms about his Lazio players.

Sources indicate that “I saw the way they were training, so I was not worried. There is a great spirit and application, we’ve got to keep going like this. It is all down to the players, they are putting in the right mentality, hunger and sense of belonging. They are doing something incredible.”.

Lazio are top of the table and still unbeaten in Serie A despite a lot of injury problems, as today they were missing Mattia Zaccagni, Nuno Tavares, Josip Sutalo and Adam Marusic.

Nicolò Rovella also came off the bench late on and is still trying to work his way back to full fitness after numerous challenges.

“Rovella can give us more vertical passes, as when he gets the ball, he immediately looks up and forward,” explained the coach.

According to recent reports, “I think we also need to talk about Fisayo Dele-Bashiru. He deserves more. We’ve got to give Rovella playing time so that he can regain fitness, then he can give us an important hand.”.

Considering how well Lazio are doing under Gattuso so far this season, is there anything he still hasn’t seen and wants them to improve?

Sources indicate that “I don’t mind losing the ball with misplaced passes that much, because when you play at a high tempo, that can happen. I am more interested in the mentality of the side and how they are hanging in there under pressure.

According to recent reports, “I am satisfied, you always want something more, but at this tempo there are going to be some misplaced passes. We can improve our reading of the game, as for example today when we struggled to get through the middle, we needed to spread the game out wide.”.

Gerry Cardinale has described Endrick as one of the best players in the world in his position, although he insists Milan’s project is bigger than any one player.

Speaking to MilanNews.it ahead of Sunday’s game against Frosinone at San Siro, the Rossoneri owner confirmed Milan will spend in January, but only on signings that fit the club’s plans.

Industry observers note that “We’re ready. We’re doing a lot of work. As we discussed, it’s complicated, and the January transfer market is always tricky, so you have to be prepared and opportunistic,” Cardinale noted. “One thing I can admit is that we’re not making any decisions we don’t feel great about. We’re going to spend money, but we’re going to spend it smartly, consistent with the project and in close coordination with Ruben and the guys here at Milanello.”.

Milan have been strongly linked with Endrick, with reports suggesting they’re ready to meet Real Madrid’s €60m valuation, but Club Brugge’s Nicolò Tresoldi is also being considered as an alternative.

Sources indicate that “Look, that name is also mentioned a lot. This project is more than just one player,” Cardinale said. “He is one of the best players, if not the best player, in the world in his position. I have a tremendous amount of respect for him. We’ll see what’s possible in the market.”.

Cardinale wouldn’t confirm Markus Krösche’s arrival as head of football. Corriere dello Sport has reported that the Eintracht Frankfurt director will start on 1 January.

Sources indicate that “You guys are very focused on Markus Krösche. That name has been bandied about. When we’re ready to make an announcement, I’ll come back to you on that.”.

He also spoke warmly about Adrien Rabiot, who is in talks over a fresh contract.

It has been revealed that “I love Adrien, he’s one of my favourite players. I think he’s fantastic, and I have a tremendous amount of respect for him and his family. We’re in discussions and I hope we’ll get a good result. If it were up to me, he’d be a franchise player for this team.”.

Fourth-placed Milan face sixth-placed Frosinone on Sunday at 18:00 CET [17:00 GMT].

“We’ve had a great couple of days and great sessions at Casa Milan on the January market, and on all our intends for the rest of this season and into next summer,” Cardinale added. “The mood here is really upbeat. We had a great practice today, and the team is really coming together. I spoke to a lot of the players, and they understand, as Ruben said, how vital this game is. Hopefully we come out strong and get the win.”.

He even suited up for Bowdoin College's JV team during his days at the Maine school. Then later, as an adult, he became a shareholder of Spanish second-division club Real Oviedo.

But his biggest impact on the sport came over the summer, when Fresh York welcomed thousands of tourists for the World Cup action at MetLife Stadium in nearby East Rutherford, New Jersey.

Upset with ticket prices for the matches, Mamdani organized more than 100 free watch parties around the city. The events were well attended and helped locals engage with the tournament even though no actual matches were played in Upcoming York.

Zohran Mamdani, center, joined by, from left, United States soccer star Tim Weah NYC World Cup Czar Maya Handa, and New York council member Yusef Salaam back in May.

Recent findings suggest that 'A kid in Corona, a nurse in Bay Ridge and a small business owner in Little Haiti could all celebrate together — for free or at a price they could afford,' he continued. 'That's what we mean when we talk about a city for the many.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that from the moment Ezri Konsa pulled on an Arsenal shirt, he has moved with all the composure of a man who knows exactly where to be and when. The centre-back has required no adaptation period in north London, where he has filled the considerable shoes of William Saliba with such class that Arsenal have hardly missed the Frenchman at all.

The loss of Saliba to a long-term back injury was supposed to be a major problem for Arsenal. Instead, the situation has now reached a point where some fans are wondering how Saliba will get back into the side. That may prove a little extreme, but the fact there is even a discussion is proof of Konsa’s superb impact at the Emirates Stadium.

“Unbelievable,” Mikel Arteta, the Arsenal manager, stated of his £55m signing. “He’s come to a huge club and to position yourself in that manner, and to perform at the level he is, it is very difficult to do. We are really lucky to have him.”.

In Arsenal’s latest victory, their seventh from eight matches in the Premier League this season, Konsa offered all of his usual defensive security and calmness in possession. Even more excitingly, he also scored his first goal for the club, smashed in from close range after a corner had caused chaos in Everton’s penalty area. It was Arsenal’s first set-piece goal of the season.

“I have been waiting to score my first goal for a while,” Konsa noted. “I spoke to the set-piece coach before the game and he told me he’s been waiting for my goal as well. We felt as players that it was coming, and today was the day.”.

Some eyebrows were raised when Arsenal paid such a large fee to sign Konsa from Aston Villa. The Villa fans, though, were not among those who questioned the price or the player’s ability. They have known for years at Villa Park that Konsa is a player of the highest quality, and they will not be surprised by his exceptional start to his Arsenal career.

The same is true of the Arsenal players. Arteta asked the England internationals in his squad about Konsa before buying him, and the feedback was overwhelmingly positive. Konsa was already close friends with Declan Rice, Bukayo Saka and Eberechi Eze before completing his transfer from Villa.

According to recent reports, konsa’s start to life at Arsenal is all the more impressive because he did not even have a pre-season. He effectively came straight from the World Cup into the club, and has been starting games since early September. His first start was against Chelsea, when he endeared himself to the home fans with a crunching tackle on former team-mate Morgan Rogers.

Industry observers note that konsa, 29, has swiftly built a strong relationship with Gabriel Magalhães, his defensive partner who scored Arsenal’s other goal here against Everton, from Ben White’s cross. For both centre-backs to find the net felt like a throwback to last year, when Arsenal were so dangerous from crosses, and underlined how Arteta’s team are capable of hurting their opponents in many different ways.

In a recent development, the nature of the goals might give a misleading impression of Arsenal’s performance, though. This was not a gritty win. Arteta’s side produced some excellent passing moves and circulated the ball with menace throughout the game. They were also a little open at times, especially in the first half when Everton created a handful of decent chances.

Thierno Barry missed the best of those opportunities, with the score at 1-0. It was the closest the visitors came to hurting the champions, aside from some of James Tarkowski’s full-blooded tackles. “I felt we didn’t really get to a level that was good enough to get near them,” admitted David Moyes, the Everton manager.

It has been revealed that the victory, combined with Manchester City’s defeat earlier in the day, put Arsenal level on points at the top of the table. Aside from the extraordinary thrashing at Brighton, Arteta’s side have looked just as solid, if not more so, than last season. That speaks volumes of the quality in the team, of course, but also notes plenty about the way Konsa has adjusted to his new surroundings. Thanks to him, Saliba’s absence has not hurt at all.

“Great feeling, it always is. A clean sheet, a goal – my first goal for the club – so a fantastic day overall.

“I’ve been waiting to score my first goal for a while. I spoke to the set piece coach before the game and he told me he’s been waiting for my goal as well, so it was only right that I got the goal today.

In a recent development, “I’ve come to this stadium for many seasons, I know how tough it is to play against us. It’s not surprising to me.

Sources indicate that “We are champions and to be champions you’ve got to win games consistently. This is our home and we want to win as many games here as possible.”.

All over at the Emirates and the champions go level on points with Manchester City at the top of the table.

According to recent reports, they kept another clean sheet and scored from a set-piece again. All is right in Arsenal’s world!

Oscar Bobb’s first Premier League goal for Fulham earned a 1-0 win over Coventry that lifted the Cottagers clear of the relegation zone.

Bobb produced a fine bit of individual skill to strike in the 80th minute as he twisted his way into the box and bent a shot into the far corner, only his second goal for the club in any competition since his £27million move from Manchester City back in January.

That was enough to give Fulham their first away win in nine attempts, a run that dated back to February, only a week after they ended their winless start to the league campaign by edging out Hull 1-0 as the pressure continues to ease on Alvaro Arbeloa.

Josh King had earlier hit the post for the visitors, who edged Coventry in just about every department to leave Frank Lampard’s side second-bottom of the table.

The hosts had only brief spells of sustained possession in Fulham’s half, but did little to trouble Bernd Leno on a frustrating afternoon which bought the CBS Arena back down to earth after their 4-1 win over Newcastle in their last home outing.

Odegaard drives a shot high over the ball as Arsenal close in on another clean sheet.

According to recent reports, probably sums up Zubimendi’s season so far that he finally gets some meaningful minutes in the Premier League and ends up getting smashed in the face and covered in his own blood. This is after he got injured in a cool-down a few weeks ago. When your luck’s out...

How have Arsenal reacted to their top scorer Saka being injured? Both of their centre backs have scored for the first time this season.

On his 200 Premier League appearance for Arsenal, Gabriel marks it with his first goal of the season.

Arsenal have defensive options in Timber, Hincapie, Calafiori and Mosquera if Arteta wants to avoid taking any risks.

A worry for Arsenal as Gabriel jars his knee into the ground as he tries to clear the ball. The Brazilian is receiving treatment and hobbles off the pitch.

Arsenal get the match restarted. The longer the match goes on without extending the lead, Everton will think they have a chance.

According to recent reports, before today, Arsenal had averaged five corners per match in the Premier League this season. In the first 45 minutes here, they had 10 corners.

The conditions are terrible at the moment. Heavy wind and rain causing havoc.

Sources indicate that A lot of set-pieces for Arsenal today as they continue to put Everton under the cosh. Can they take advantage of their dominance again before the break?

Arsenal have found their groove again, with Madueke twice going close to extending their lead. Rice, Lewis-Skelly, Odegaard and Merino are forming a box in midfield and Everton don’t seem to know how to shut them down.

Another effort at goal for Madueke. This one is a snapshot from the edge of the box that goes into the side netting.

Courtesy of Opta: Arsenal scored their first set-piece goal in all competitions (not including penalties) since May of last season against Crystal Palace, ending a run of 13 games without one.

Horrible conditions at the Emirates today. The rain has been lashing down. The Emirates drainage system is usually able to cope with this sort of thing. If the wind picks up, that’s likely to be a bigger problem for the two teams.

On bouncing back from defeat...

“Yeah, we’ve had a good start. Obviously, we had a bit of a blip last week against Chelsea. I don’t think we, as a team, won first and second balls enough and that’s something the manager wants us to get back to today. You’ve got to win your battles.”.

On what makes Arsenal difficult to play...

Sources indicate that “They’re reigning Premier League champions, a top side that has been knocking on the door to win the title for a few years before as well. They’re a team at a high level but this is what Premier League football is all about and it’s up to us to get a result.”.

It has been revealed that “Well, we play every two-and-a-half days so we didn’t have much time to recover, so we need full energy. There are certain specific players as well that they fit really well for the game that we expect today and that’s how we start.”.

“A very competitive team, a really well organised team. I think that it’s very clear what they want to do, where they want to take the game. The threats, when they have a space to run, any time that they are able to put the ball in their box, you know the presence and aggression that they have. So, yeah, we have to really be at it and be very aggressive from the beginning.”.

One of the clearest signs a football club is in a good place is when the debate switches from whether the team are winning to how they are winning.

This is currently Arsenal and Mikel Arteta’s world. For years, Arsenal coaches and players were asked how and when they would start collecting major trophies again. With no concern about their capacity to challenge for top honours over the coming years, the style has become the main focus.

It has been revealed that it’s a welcome “problem” – or some might argue a non-existent one – for Arteta while his side is so strong. Building a fortress is the expensive, time-consuming and difficult part. Once it’s constructed and established, how you decorate it is a matter of taste.

Whether neutrals will hold the current champions in the same regard as the great Arsène Wenger sides will be a trivial concern if Arteta does what no Arsenal manager has since 1935 – defend the league title – and then add a few more, which is a serious possibility based on the balance of power in England and the likely punishment heading Manchester City’s way.

Industry observers note that today there will be tributes to Ken Friar, who passed away at the age of 92 earlier this year. Advertising boards outside the Emirates Stadium have been taken over by images of Friar, who had a remarkable 70-year association with the club.

In today’s programme, captain Martin Odegaard has written the following: “It’s exceptional people like Ken Friar who have built the club into what it is today, and we as the current team are the ones privileged to continue his legacy.”.

This is a first Premier League start of the season for Viktor Gyokeres, who has been behind Kai Havertz in the pecking order over the past few months. Gyokeres has yet to score in nine appearances in all competitions this season, although he would (understandably) make the point that it’s harder to do so when you are coming off the bench late in games.

For Arsenal, Arteta shuffles his team after the draw against Bayern: White, Lewis-Skelly, Merino, Eze and Gyokeres start.

Max Dowman, who scored a memorable goal in this fixture last season, is on the bench.

For Everton, Jack Grealish misses today’s game due to sickness, while Jarrad Branthwaite is absent because of concussion protocols despite finishing last week’s match with Chelsea after a head collision with Emi Martinez.

Arsenal: Raya, White, Gabriel, Konsa, Lewis-Skelly, Rice, Merino, Odegaard, Madueke, Eze, Gyokeres.Subs: Arrizabalaga, Timber, Hincapie, Calafiori, Mosquera, Zubimendi, Guimaraes, Dowman, Havertz.

Everton: Pickford, Tarkowski, O’Brien, Armstrong, Rohl, Dewsbury-Hall, George, Barry, Garner, Mykolenko, JohnsonSubs: Travers, King, Maitland-Niles, Keane, Dibling, Norgaard, Alcaraz, Hackney, Braiden Graham.

Hello and welcome to coverage from the Emirates as Premier League champions Arsenal host Everton.

Mikel Arteta’s men produced a good performance in midweek to draw with Bayern Munich in the Champions League while David Moyes’s squad have had the week off following their 2-0 defeat by Chelsea last weekend.

Arteta said: “We’re having three games in six days so we know what’s happening, especially when the games are so demanding and the necessity is to win. We know that, so we prepare the players for those scenarios and do the best we possibly can.

Industry observers note that “I know David so well and how he sets the team, the quality they have in their organisation and individually. It’s no coincidence they didn’t lose before their last game. They have a really good team, which we know because in recent clashes, it’s always been a really difficult game for us.”.

Both teams enter this game having been beaten just once this season but eight points separate them with Arsenal in second and Everton in eighth.

Moyes remarked: “It’s not an easy game and never has been over many years. We look forward to it; they had a game in midweek, and we have to try and capitalise on that. I thought we did really well last year against them; we played really well down at Arsenal, and I hope we can do the same.

Recent findings suggest that “When I look back at the team we had out, we were pretty threadbare at that time, but we did a good job, and I hope we can do it again. Obviously Arsenal have some many different tools in their bag and people they can use in different positions, so we’re fully aware of the team we’re up against and the level.”.

Former Arsenal players Ainsley Maitland-Niles and Christian Norgaard could feature for Everton this afternoon.

New Manchester United head coach Mauricio Pochettino has been tipped to make Fulham defender Antonee Robinson his very first signing at Old Trafford.

That is according to a report from Football Insider, which claims that the left-back has been on the radar of the Red Devils for quite some time and continues to be high on their list of transfer targets.

Having worked closely with the 29-year-old during his tenure in charge of the United States national team, including all four matches of the 2026 FIFA World Cup, Pochettino is reportedly eager to reunite with the defender.

Speaking on Football Insider’s Transfer Insider podcast, transfer correspondent Pete O’Rourke explained why Robinson sits right at the top of Pochettino’s winter shortlist:.

“Yeah, of course, there’ll always be speculation about which players Mauricio Pochettino could look to bring in. Like you said, Antonee Robinson has been a long-term target for United and obviously United do have complications at left back as well.

According to recent reports, “And with Luke Shaw’s contract coming up to expire in the summer as well, they’re going to have to do something in that area to try and improve this team. Robinson is somebody they have been looking at for a while, and if Pochettino wants to recruit some former players, he will be high on that list for him I’m sure.”.

Left-back has become an urgent priority for Manchester United’s recruitment team.

With Luke Shaw’s contract set to expire at the end of the season and ongoing fitness concerns continuing to disrupt the squad’s defensive stability, Pochettino requires an athletic, durable full-back capable of executing his high-pressing, overlapping system from day one.

Diogo Dalot has also failed to impress this season, with his performances coming under criticism both at left-back and right-back.

Robinson, who has already made over 220 senior appearances for Fulham and ranks among the Premier League’s most relentless runners, fits that profile seamlessly.

United’s admiration for the Milton Keynes-born American is not new.

Having previously registered a remarkable 10-assist Premier League campaign in 2024/25, Robinson has remained firmly on Old Trafford’s radar.

With Fulham tying him down until June 2028, and rival clubs such as Liverpool, Chelsea, and Newcastle United also monitoring his situation, Pochettino’s personal relationship with Robinson could prove decisive if United launch a formal bid worth £25 million or more in January.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Towards the end of their lives, stars experience a drastic change in their structure as they swell and enter what is known as their giant phase. Because most stars are thought to host orbiting companions (such as planets, other stars or black holes), interesting interactions can happen as the giant host expands. The most striking of these occur when a companion star is engulfed by a giant: astronomers refer to this as the common-envelope phase1. Despite theoretical expectations that common envelopes should be widespread in stellar evolution, they have been extraordinarily difficult to observe. Writing in Nature, however, Karambelkar et al.2 report the first direct detection of a star inside a giant star.

Why Everton School Visits Are Making A Mark

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
